content.body: Have you ever used a calculator where you type numbers and operators like 3 4 +? That's Reverse Polish Notation! Today we'll learn to evaluate these expressions efficiently. We'll use a clever approach that remembers what we've already seen to process everything in one pass.
content.title: Welcome

content.body:
• Apply a stack-based approach to evaluate arithmetic expressions
• Implement the algorithm using array iteration and conditional logic
• Explain why this approach processes each element exactly once
• Handle different arithmetic operators (+, -, *, /) correctly
• Return the final integer result from the expression
content.title: What you'll learn

content.body: Let's start with a simple expression. Which two numbers would you add first in this expression: 3 4 + 2 * ?
content.title: Try it
content.prompt: What's the first calculation you'd do?
content.successMessage: Exactly! You'd add 3 and 4 first to get 7.

content.title: Try a longer expression
content.successMessage: Great! You started with 1 + 2 = 3, then 3 * 4 = 12, then 5 + 12 = 17, then 17 - 3 = 14.

content.title: One more challenge
content.successMessage: Perfect! You're working through the expression step by step, keeping track of intermediate results.

content.body: What you just did was mental calculation - you kept track of numbers in your head, performed operations when you saw operators, and remembered intermediate results. This works for small expressions but gets hard with many operations.
content.title: What you did

content.body: When expressions have dozens of operations, keeping everything in your head is challenging. We need a systematic method that remembers intermediate results automatically. Can't figure it out? Click Show me on the next step.
content.title: Why it gets hard

content.body: The key insight is to use a structure that remembers what we've already seen - specifically, the numbers we've processed. Think of it like a notebook where we write down numbers as we encounter them, and when we see an operator, we look back at the last two numbers we wrote to perform the calculation.
content.title: Key idea
content.visualMetaphor: A notebook where we write down what we've seen and check it in one step.

content.body: We'll use a stack (like a pile of plates) to remember numbers. As we go through the expression: if it's a number, we add it to our stack; if it's an operator, we take the last two numbers from the stack, perform the operation, and put the result back. This way we only need to look at each element once!
content.title: The approach
content.illustratedExample:
Walkthrough with ["2", "1", "+", "3", "*"]:
1. See '2' → push 2 to stack: [2]
2. See '1' → push 1 to stack: [2, 1]
3. See '+' → pop 1 and 2, calculate 2 + 1 = 3, push 3: [3]
4. See '3' → push 3: [3, 3]
5. See '*' → pop 3 and 3, calculate 3 * 3 = 9, push 9: [9]
Final result: 9

content.body:
1. Create an empty stack to store numbers
2. Loop through each element in the expression
3. If the element is a number, convert it to integer and push to stack
4. If it's an operator (+, -, *, /), pop the last two numbers
5. Perform the operation (note: for subtraction and division, the order matters!)
6. Push the result back to the stack
7. After the loop, the stack should have one number - return it
content.title: Steps

steps.title: Create the function and stack
steps.instruction: Start by creating the function that takes the tokens array. Inside, create an empty array that will serve as our stack to remember numbers.
steps.hint: The stack is just an array where we'll push and pop numbers.
steps.expectedOutcome: A function with an empty stack array
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! You've set up the basic structure. The stack will help us remember numbers as we process them.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're on the right track. Make sure you create an empty array inside the function.
steps.feedbackWrong: Remember: we need an array to store numbers. Try creating an empty array variable.

steps.title: Loop through tokens
steps.instruction: Add a loop to go through each token in the input array. We'll process each element one by one.
steps.hint: Use a for...of loop to iterate through the tokens array.
steps.expectedOutcome: A loop that iterates through tokens
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Now we can examine each element of the expression.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost there. Make sure you're looping through the tokens parameter.
steps.feedbackWrong: We need to process each token. Try using for (let token of tokens) { ... }

steps.title: Handle numbers
steps.instruction: Inside the loop, check if the current token is a number. If it is, convert it to an integer and push it onto the stack. Remember: tokens are strings, so we need to check if it's not an operator.
steps.hint: You can check if token is NOT one of the operators: '+', '-', '*', '/'
steps.expectedOutcome: Condition that pushes numbers to stack
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Now numbers get remembered in our stack.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good start. Make sure you convert the token to a number before pushing.
steps.feedbackWrong: For numbers, we need to push them to the stack. Try: if (token !== '+' && token !== '-' && token !== '*' && token !== '/') { stack.push(Number(token)); }

steps.title: Handle operators - pop numbers
steps.instruction: Add an else clause for when token is an operator. First, pop the last two numbers from the stack. Important: the second pop is the first operand, and the first pop is the second operand!
steps.hint: Use stack.pop() twice and store the values in variables.
steps.expectedOutcome: Code that pops two values from stack for operators
steps.feedbackCorrect: Great! Now we have the numbers ready for calculation.
steps.feedbackPartial: You're close. Remember to pop twice and store both values.
steps.feedbackWrong: For operators, we need two numbers. Try: const b = stack.pop(); const a = stack.pop();

steps.title: Perform calculations
steps.instruction: Now perform the appropriate calculation based on the operator. Use a switch statement or if-else to handle +, -, *, and /. Remember: for subtraction, it's a - b, and for division, it's a / b with integer division (truncate toward zero).
steps.hint: The order matters: a (first pop) and b (second pop). Use Math.trunc() for division.
steps.expectedOutcome: Switch or if-else that calculates result for each operator
steps.feedbackCorrect: Perfect! Now we can handle all four basic operations.
steps.feedbackPartial: Good progress. Make sure you handle all four operators and use Math.trunc() for division.
steps.feedbackWrong: Try using switch(token) with cases for each operator. For division: result = Math.trunc(a / b);

steps.title: Return the final result
steps.instruction: After the loop finishes, the stack should contain exactly one number - the final result. Return this number.
steps.hint: The result is the only element left in the stack array.
steps.expectedOutcome: Return statement that returns the final value from stack
steps.feedbackCorrect: Excellent! Your function is complete and ready to evaluate expressions.
steps.feedbackPartial: Almost done. The final result is in the stack - you need to return it.
steps.feedbackWrong: After processing all tokens, return stack[0] or stack.pop().

content.body: Great work! You've implemented the Reverse Polish Notation evaluator using a stack to remember numbers. Key takeaways: 1) The stack helps us remember intermediate results efficiently, 2) We process each token exactly once (O(n) time), 3) The order of operands matters for subtraction and division. This 'remember what we've seen' pattern is powerful for many algorithm problems!
content.title: Done
